While the amendment is incidental, the panel’s reissuance of its  Barbosa  opinion provides an ideal segue to our first topic: How the Supreme Court’s recent decision in  United States v. Davis bolsters a  cause celebre on the Ninth Circuit—namely, the growing belief that deporting aliens for “crimes involving moral turpitude” (CIMT) is unconstitutional.

  On 3rd July, the full Ninth Circuit voted to rehear  State of California v. Azar .

  As I reported in the prior section, the Ninth Circuit agreed to rehear California v. Azar before an  en banc panel. Because the Ninth Circuit is so large, its  en banc panels consist of eleven judges, rather than the whole court.  California v. Azar was a  per curiam  order, which made me curious whether the original three judges would participate in the  en banc rehearing. According to the court’s rules, however, the eleven judges will be drawn from the total pool of active judges. (See Rule 35–3 & accompanying notes ). The upshot is that the government won unanimously before a three-judge panel, but could (theoretically) lose unanimously before an  en banc panel.

  A similarly wacky outcome is implicated by the  en banc dynamics of a Ninth Circuit panel’s order in  Torres v. Barr , an immigration controversy that was decided on 12th June. In  Torres , the court sided with the government out of respect for circuit precedent. Nonetheless, all 3 judges on the  Torres panel joined a concurring opinion arguing that the circuit’s precedent was wrongly decided. Yet only an  en banc court can overturn a three-judge panel’s precedent. It follows that if the full court were to vote against an  en banc rehearing, then the petitioner in  Torres would have persuaded a unanimous three-judge panel on the merits, yet still lost.

When the Legislature advanced the No Vigilantes Act, the Peace Officers Research Association of California warned that the measure was constitutionally defective and would not survive judicial review. On October 14, 2026, the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit confirmed that assessment. In a published opinion in United States v. State of California, No. 26-926 (9th Cir. Oct. 14, 2026), the panel reversed the district court and ordered entry of a preliminary injunction against enforcement of Section 10 of the No Vigilantes Act, S.B. 805, holding that the statute cannot be applied to the United States, its agencies, or its officers. The unanimous panel, speaking through Judge Bennett, concluded that the United States is certain to succeed on the merits of its Supremacy Clause claim. California enacted the No Vigilantes Act (S.B. 805) on September 20, 2025, in response to federal immigration enforcement efforts.
On November 17, 2025, the United States sued California, Governor Gavin Newsom, and Attorney General Rob Bonta, facially challenging §§ 2 and 10 of the No Vigilantes Act and §§ 2 and 3 of the No Secret Police Act under the Supremacy Clause. The district court denied preliminary relief as to § 10, finding the United States had not shown its identification practices were essential to federal operations, but it enjoined § 3 of the No Secret Police Act; no party appealed that ruling. The United States appealed only the § 10 denial.  
While the appeal was pending, the Ninth Circuit entered a temporary administrative injunction on February 19, 2026, and granted an injunction pending appeal on April 22, 2026. The same panel, assigned under General Order 6.4(d), then decided the merits and adopted its prior analysis for precedential purposes.
Writing for the panel, Judge Bennett held the United States was certain to succeed on its facial Supremacy Clause challenge. Because the challenge was facial and brought before any enforcement, the United States had to show that no set of circumstances exists under which § 10 would be valid. On April 22, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit handed the federal government a significant legal victory in its escalating conflict with California over immigration enforcement transparency. The court issued an injunction blocking California's **No Vigilantes Act** (SB 805) — specifically Section 10, which required non-uniformed federal law enforcement officers to wear visible identification during operations. The ruling deepens a constitutional fault line between state authority and federal supremacy that has been cracking since immigration agents in unmarked vehicles began conducting operations across the state.

This isn't just about ID badges. It's a proxy battle over who controls how federal law enforcement operates on American soil — and the Ninth Circuit just delivered a clear, if preliminary, answer.

## What the Ninth Circuit Actually Ruled

The Ninth Circuit's injunction, issued in the case *United States v. State of California*, blocks California Governor Gavin Newsom and Attorney General Rob Bonta from applying or enforcing Section 10 of the No Vigilantes Act against federal agencies and officers while the appeal proceeds. This is a preliminary injunction — not a final ruling on the merits — but its reasoning signals how the court views the constitutional stakes.

The court found the California law **likely violates the Supremacy Clause** of the U.S. Constitution, which establishes federal law as the supreme law of the land and generally prohibits states from directly regulating federal operations. ## What is United States v. California? A 30-Second Summary

Imagine a massive apartment building where the building manager (the federal government) sets the rules for who is allowed on the property. Now, imagine the renter of the largest, most influential apartment (California) decides they don't want to help the manager evict people. They don't actively stop the manager, but they instruct their own staff not to report residents or help with the eviction process unless a serious crime is involved. This creates a tense standoff. The building manager claims their authority over the entire property is being undermined, while the renter argues they have the right to control their own staff within their own apartment. This is the essence of **United States v. California**, a landmark legal battle over immigration enforcement. It wasn't just a lawsuit; it was a high-stakes constitutional clash between the Trump administration and the State of California over its “sanctuary” laws. The core question was profound: Can the federal government force a state to use its own resources—its police, its jails, its employees—to help enforce federal immigration laws? The Supreme Court's answer reshaped the modern understanding of states' rights and federal power.

corpus.title: United States v. Oakland Cannabis Buyers' Cooperative
corpus.snippet: In United States v. Oakland Cannabis Buyers' Cooperative, 532 U.S. 483 (2001), the United States Supreme Court rejected the common-law medical necessity defense to crimes enacted under the federal Controlled Substances Act of 1970,[1] regardless of their legal status under the laws of states such as California that recognize a medical use for marijuana.[2] Oakland Cannabis Buyers' Cooperative was represented by Gerald Uelmen.
